items.stem: An application keeps each user's login session in the memory of the machine that handled the login. The team adds a second machine behind a load balancer that uses round robin. What do users experience?

options.text: Some users are logged out at random.
options.feedback: A user who logs in on machine 1 may send the next request to machine 2, which has no record of the login. The session data has to be kept outside the application machine.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the two machines share their memory.
options.feedback: Each machine has its own memory, and machines do not share it automatically.

options.text: The site goes down, because a load balancer needs a single machine.
options.feedback: A load balancer is designed for several machines. The problem comes from where the application keeps the session data.

items.stem: Before you try it: machine E is four times slower than the others and the load balancer uses round robin. While traffic is running, what will the in-progress counts show?

options.text: About the same number on every machine.
options.feedback: Round robin gives every machine the same number of requests, but E finishes them more slowly, so its requests pile up.

options.text: More requests in progress on E than on the others.
options.feedback: Every machine receives the same number of requests, and E takes four times as long to finish each one. Requests accumulate on E.

options.text: Fewer requests in progress on E, because it is slower.
options.feedback: A slower machine holds each request for longer, so more of them are in progress at the same time.

items.try: Press Send traffic with round robin selected and watch the in-progress count on E. Then switch to least connections.

items.stem: Machine C crashes while the load balancer is running health checks. What happens to requests after the next failed check?

options.text: The load balancer stops using C and the other machines take its share.
options.feedback: This is what a health check is for. A few requests sent before the check fails may get errors, but after that users are not affected.

options.text: Every request fails until an engineer restarts machine C by hand.
options.feedback: The load balancer routes around a machine that fails its health check.

options.text: Requests wait in the load balancer until C passes its health check again.
options.feedback: The load balancer sends requests to machines that are working. It does not hold requests for a failed machine.

items.stem: Before you try it: the load is 400 requests per second, each machine handles 80, and each request needs 3 database queries. The database handles 300 queries per second. You turn on the load balancer and set 5 application machines. Which part limits the system now?

options.feedback: Five machines handle 5 × 80 = 400 requests per second, which is enough for the load.
At 3 queries per request, 300 queries per second allows only 100 requests per second. Five machines can send far more than that.
The load balancer is not the limit in this model. The database is.

items.try: Turn on the load balancer, set Application machines to 5 and read the verdict.

items.stem: The database is the bottleneck: 3 queries per request and 300 queries per second allow only 100 requests per second. Which change raises the limit the most?

options.text: Add a cache for 70% of the reads.
options.feedback: Only 30% of the queries reach the database, which is 0.9 queries per request. The database can then serve about 333 requests per second.
The machines are not the limit. More of them would send more queries to the same database.
A faster handler helps the application machines, but the limit here is the number of queries the database can answer.
